overview: The Tibetan Empire rose under Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century and for two hundred years matched Tang China and the Arab caliphate for control of the Silk Road, from the Tarim Basin to the Himalaya. It gave Tibet its script, its first monasteries and its Buddhism.

items.text: Songtsen Gampo married Princess Wencheng of Tang, who brought a Buddha image and texts to Lhasa; a Nepalese princess, Bhrikuti, is remembered as his other Buddhist queen.
The Tibetan script was created, by tradition by Thonmi Sambhota, from an Indian script of the Gupta type.
Samye, the first Tibetan Buddhist monastery, was completed under Trisong Detsen, and Buddhism spread beside the native Bon rites.
The Jokhang temple was built in Lhasa and became Tibet's holiest shrine.
Tibetan armies fielded armored cavalry and took fortified towns with methods learned from China and Central Asia.
Tibet held the Tarim oases and, from 786 to 848, Dunhuang, taxing the Silk Road between China, India and Central Asia.
A Tibetan army occupied the Tang capital Chang'an for about two weeks.
A peace treaty with Tang was carved in Tibetan and Chinese on a pillar that still stands outside the Jokhang.
The Tibetan script is in use today across Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalaya.
Buddhism became the core of Tibetan identity and culture.

fall.text: The emperor Langdarma was assassinated in 842 and the empire broke into rival kingdoms, the Era of Fragmentation, that lasted until the eleventh century.
